transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-04-28
Time: 08:00 PT / 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Alex Kim (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (Redwood SRE), Samir Patel (Redwood Support); Maya Chen (AtlasAI ML Lead), Diego Ramos (AtlasAI Infra), Lena Novak (AtlasAI CTO), Arjun Shah (AtlasAI Backend)

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on recurring OOMs and transient CUDA timeouts seen during AtlasAI nightly batch and peak inference window. Discussed batching behavior, KV cache interactions, quantization tradeoffs, driver/kernel versions, and retry semantics (idempotency, backoff, circuit breakers). Agreed on repro steps, logs to collect, and immediate mitigation options (reduce batch size, limit concurrency, enable KV eviction, consider int8/4-bit quantization).

Topics: OOM patterns, CUDA error traces, timeout semantics, retry logic and idempotency, batching heuristics, KV cache eviction, quantization offload, VPC/on-prem constraints for diag artifacts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro then dive into the OOM traces we got from Atlas.
[00:18] Maya: cool thanks, our main pain is that in prod over the last two weeks we see intermittent OOMs during peak HH (around 3-4AM UTC) and sometimes the request just times out and client sees a 504. we've attached a heap of logs but they look like CUDA cuBLAS failures in places.
[00:35] Alex: yeah thanks, we looked at the initial stack traces; there's a pattern where higher sequence lengths + dynamic batching spikes memory use because the KV cache grows across concurrent streams. sometimes the runtime can't reclaim kv quickly enough and we hit the GPU allocator OOM.
[00:55] Diego: just to add, we didn't change the model recently, we updated a small change in our batching layer end of last month. also sequence length distribution has a heavy tail, some prompts go to 12k tokens.
[01:12] Priya: (clarifying) when you say "KV cache grows" are you referring to per-request kv caching or shared prefix cache?
[01:20] Alex: good q. Atlas is using prefix KV cache for common system prompts plus per-session caching. the runtime keeps per-shard kv in GPU memory and with concurrent sessions and large seq lengths it adds up. there's also evict heuristics but on amd spike they lag.
[01:36] Maya: evict heuristics lag? like eviction not fast enough?
[01:40] Alex: yeah, when concurrent requests suddenly increase the kernel scheduler doesn't preempt the kv usage immediately; by the time eviction happens the allocator had already rejected the new allocation, which surfaces as an OOM in the CUDA allocator.
[01:54] Lena: we also see driver resets occasionally in the same window - does that align?
[01:58] Samir: yep, driver reset can follow severe OOMs; NV driver will kill the process or reset the GPU which then shows as a cudart/cudaDriver error. I've seen logs where the process gets a 701 or 704-like error string then a timeout.
[02:12] Arjun: can the runtime fall back to CPU for the KV and keep serving?
[02:16] Alex: not automatically today; we have an experimental host-KV-offload that pages some KV to host memory, but that's slower and can increase latency. fallback would be a graceful degrade path where we reduce batch size or serve a smaller model.
[02:30] Jordan: let's talk retry semantics; Atlas observed retries making load worse because clients automatically retry 3x on timeouts. that caused cascading load spikes.
[02:40] Diego: oh yeah that was us — our frontend retries on 504 without jitter. we realized many of those were amplifying the problem.
[02:46] Priya: so we recommend idempotent retry with exponential backoff plus a request dedupe at the client for non-idempotent calls. also server-side circuit breaker to short-circuit when memory pressure thresholds exceed X.
[02:58] Maya: do you have recommended thresholds? e g what memory free threshold should trip the breaker?
[03:04] Alex: from our benchmarks, for Atlas's model size (~13B quantized to 4-bit), keep per-GPU free memory >= 1.5 GB under load to avoid eviction storms. trip at 1.2 GB for circuit-breaker and start shedding or falling back.
[03:20] Lena: we're running 80 GB A100s, but because of multi-tenant pools other workloads sometimes squeeze memory. how do we isolate?
[03:28] Priya: Reserved capacity or dedicated pools are good; for private deployments you can pin a model to a node or set cgroup-like limits. part of Redwood Dedicated is per-customer GPU pools so noisy neighbors won't be an issue.
[03:40] Arjun: what about quantization — we tried 8-bit and saw big memory wins but some accuracy drop. is 4-bit safe?
[03:48] Alex: 4-bit (GPTQ/awq) gives more memory but may need calibration for your prompt patterns; there's tradeoff. For stability, mixed approach: critical endpoints use 8-bit or full fp16, and background/low-stability endpoints use 4-bit to save headroom. also using grouped quantization can help.
[04:08] Diego: there's also a pattern where at the end of long sequences the KV cache spikes when generating. can we stream KV or evict prefixes?
[04:15] Alex: yes, options: eager prefix eviction, limit max cache per-session, or compress older KV. Runtime supports TTL-based KV eviction; tuning TTL and eviction aggressiveness helps. Also you can enable prefix trimming for sessions expected to be long.
[04:30] Maya: ok what about timeouts — we see 30s timeouts at the LB level leading to retries. is there a way to surface partial tokens to the client?
[04:38] Jordan: streaming tokens reduces perceived latency and reduces client-side retries; if you stream early tokens, clients may not retry. also configure LB timeout slightly higher during peak or use 202 Accepted + async poll if you expect long tails.
[04:52] Arjun: on the CUDA errors — some traces show cublasLt/blas deep error messages and then a "context destroyed" snippet, is that driver or application?
[04:58] Samir: usually a downstream of OOM. cublas can fail when workspace allocation fails, then subsequent calls see invalid context. also if kernel is stuck past watchdog timeout on host, the driver can reset which triggers context lost.
[05:15] Diego: watchdog timeout? are we hitting kernel-level watchdogs?
[05:18] Priya: on single-GPU nodes with display driver the GPU can have a TDR (timeout detection recovery) if kernels run too long. but in datacenter GPUs the watchdog is usually disabled; more common cause is memory allocation failure followed by kernel crash.
[05:30] Maya: what logs should we send you to help root cause?
[05:34] Alex: nvml logs, dmesg around the time, runtime debug logs (redwood-inference logs), per-request mem snapshots, and the model parameter/quantization config. also the client trace (timestamps of retries).
[05:47] Maya: we'll upload those to the shared S3 link.
[05:50] Jordan: good. let's cover immediate mitigations you can try now to reduce OOM surface: 1) reduce max batch size and enable batch timeout shorter, 2) cap concurrent requests per-server (soft limit), 3) aggressive KV eviction TTL change, 4) consider 8-bit quantization for critical routes, 5) add jittered exponential backoff on client retries, 6) server-side circuit breaker based on free memory metric.
[06:12] Arjun: how much will reducing batch size hurt throughput? we need to balance cost.
[06:16] Alex: depends on your latency SLO. for Atlas's workload with many long tails, smaller batches can actually reduce retries and net throughput loss might be small. our suggestion is dynamic batching: keep batch size adaptive with upper bound and latency cap.
[06:31] Diego: dynamic batching - is that on the runtime side or client side?
[06:34] Alex: runtime side — we have a batcher that coalesces requests within a latency window; you can set both latency cap and max batch size per model. tuning those reduces memory spikes.
[06:44] Lena: anything around kernel/driver versions? we run 525.xx drivers.
[06:48] Samir: we recommend recent stable drivers that match CUDA runtime — 535+ or the distro-backed versions on Ubuntu 22.04 tends to be stable. we'll correlate your dmesg with known driver issues. I'll open a support ticket.
[07:02] Maya: re retry semantics again — what's Redwood's default behavior now?
[07:06] Jordan: server returns 5xx on internal failure; Redwood clients default to no automatic retrys to be safe, but many customers have their own client that retries. we recommend client retries only for idempotent requests and with exponential backoff + jitter, and server-side rate-limits to avoid amplification.
[07:22] Diego: is there a token-level cost difference when using quantized models vs fp16? we saw cost numbers but want to confirm memory vs latency trade offs.
[07:29] Alex: quantized models reduce memory significantly but may increase compute (dequantization overhead), so latency could slightly increase for some kernels; however the net throughput per GPU usually improves because you fit more concurrent sessions. also for certain kernels we use fused int8 kernels that are actually faster.
[07:45] Maya: you mentioned host-KV-offload earlier, is that production-ready?
[07:49] Priya: it's experimental in our private deployments; it pushes older KV pages to host pinned memory and fetches on demand. it works but increases tail latency; we can test with your traffic shape.
[07:59] Arjun: about VPC/on-prem — we can't share S3 logs over internet, anything we need from you for debugging?
[08:04] Jordan: for private deployments we'll accept logs via secure SFTP or a support bundle exported via the console; we also have a private agent you can run to gather nvml/dmesg and redact PII.
[08:17] Diego: great. any long-term infra changes you recommend?
[08:20] Alex: 1) move to dedicated pools for critical endpoints, 2) add horizontal capacity to smooth spikes, 3) implement server-side shedding and graceful degradation to smaller model under memory pressure, 4) post-deploy load testing for long-tail seq lengths.
[08:36] Maya: we want to reproduce locally — what's the simplest repro?
[08:39] Alex: easiest: use a synthetic client that sends mixed-length sequences with the same distribution you see, with concurrency similar to peak, and enable debug mem snapshots per request. we can share a repro harness.
[08:48] Jordan: action items recap: Alex will collect nvml and runtime logs; Priya will run a high-concurrency sim; Maya will share prompt set; Samir open ticket for drivers. we'll regroup after logs and proposed config changes.
[08:58] Lena: one more question: if we hit a driver reset, what's expected behavior on Redwood Dedicated vs Private?
[09:04] Priya: Redwood Dedicated: process is restarted orchestrator-level and requests route to other healthy replicas if autoscaling/burst is configured. In Private deployments, behavior depends on your orchestrator — we provide docs for liveness probes and auto-restart policies.
[09:18] Arjun: ok thanks, that helps.
[09:22] Maya: thanks everyone, will follow up with artifacts.
[09:26] Jordan: thanks all — we'll send proposed config changes and a plan for bench test.

Notes about transcript quality: some speaker labels and proper nouns might be slightly off, a few technical terms transcribed with small errors (eg "kv cash" instead of KV cache).

Appendix - Diagnostic checklist shared on call:
- nvml snapshot around failure timestamp
- dmesg and kernel logs
- runtime (redwood) debug logs and per-request mem snapshots
- model config (quantization, group size, fp16/8/4 settings)
- network/load profile (TPS, concurrency, seq len dist)
- client retry behavior and LB timeout settings

End of transcript.
